Al Gore was the forty-fifth Vice President of the United States, serving under Bill Clinton from nineteen ninety-three to two thousand one. During his tenure, he presided over the longest period of economic expansion in American history and the push toward government surpluses in the late nineteen nineties. Gore lost the two thousand presidential election in one of the closest and most controversial elections in American history, decided by the Supreme Court's intervention in Bush v. Gore. Before becoming Vice President, he served as a U.S. Senator from Tennessee, where he advocated for environmental protection and arms control. As Vice President, Gore championed technological innovation and the information superhighway as part of Clinton's modernization agenda, helping shape early internet policy. After leaving office, he authored An Inconvenient Truth, a book and documentary film published in two thousand six that brought climate science to popular audiences and earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in two thousand seven. He established an activist organization called the Climate Reality Project, positioning himself as the world's leading voice on climate change and renewable energy. Though he nearly ran for president again in two thousand eight, he ultimately declined, focusing instead on environmental and humanitarian causes. Gore's legacy shifted from electoral politics to environmental activism, making him the world's most prominent climate change advocate.
